Palladium-Catalyzed Synthesis of 1 ‑Vinyltetrahydro-β-carbolines
and Aza-spiroindolenines: Access to the Syntheses of 1 ‑Vinyl-β-
carbolines and Eudistomins Y1 and Y2
Amrita Mondal and Chinmay Chowdhury *
Cite This: J. Org. Chem. 2021, 86, 3810 −3825 Read Online
ACCESS Metrics & More Article Recommendations *sı Supporting Information
ABSTRACT: A general synthesis of 1-vinyltetrahydro- β-carbo-
lines (THBCs) has been achieved via palladium(0)-catalyzed
cyclocondensation between allenyltryptamines and aryl iodides.
Aza-spiroindolenines could also be accessed from the N-
unsubstituted indole substrates by simply tweaking the reaction
conditions. DDQ-mediated oxidation of THBCs easily a ﬀorded β-
carbolines, which could be synthetically transformed into 1-aroyl- β-
carbolines of pharmacological interest. Formal total syntheses of
eudistomins Y1 and Y2 have also been achieved.
■ INTRODUCTION
The tetrahydro- β-carboline (THBC; 1, Figure 1 ) and β-
carboline (BC; 2, Figure 1 ) ring systems, considered as
privileged heterocycles, have attracted substantial attention as
synthetic targets because of their presence as core structure in
a large number of biologically active and structurally diverse
alkaloids and synthetic compounds
1a,f including pharmaceut-
icals and their utilization as a popular template in drug
discovery programs.
1g Incorporation of a vinyl moiety at the
C1 position of both THBCs and BCs proved to be e ﬃcacious
in improving the pharmacological e ﬀects in a number of
compounds. For example, the fungal toxin f umitremorgin C
(3a, Figure 1 ) proves to be a potent and speci ﬁc inhibitor of
breast cancer resistant protein 2a (BCRP/ABCG2) multidrug
transporter, while the demethoxy analogue 3b (Figure 1 )
eﬀectively arrests the cell cycle 2b (at G2/M phase), indicating
its implication in cancer therapy. In the recent past, screening
of a number of derivatives of the alkaloid harmine identi ﬁed
the β-carboline derivative 4 as a potent anticancer lead, 2c while
5 emerged as a highly potent, orally bioavailable antimalarial
agent.2d
Among the large number of THBCs, C1-substituted
derivatives widely exist in nature as a constituent of indole
alkaloids; consequently, there have been many reports 3 on
their syntheses including those involving modern transition-
metal catalysts ( Scheme 1 ). Most of them adopted the well-
known Pictet−Spengler (PS) reaction, 4 which however proves
less useful when 1-vinyl-substituted THBCs are targeted. Only
a few reports
5 exist where N-allyl,5a allenyl,5b or propargyl 5c
derivatives of tryptamine were exposed to rhodium, gold and
palladium catalyst respectively ( Scheme 1 a−c), besides other
methods5d,e employing oxidative C(sp 3)−H ole ﬁnation at the
C1 position of the preformed THBCs. Consequently, the
applications of C1-vinyl THBCs in medicinal chemistry or
other ﬁelds are limited. Therefore, development of a
straightforward and practical method for the general synthesis
of C1-vinyl-substituted THBCs remains worthwhile. It is
interesting to note that substrates utilized in the formation of
THBCs or the compounds resembling the structure of those

ﬁeld resulting in the generation of indole fused products D−J
(Scheme 1 d,e).
On the other hand, C1-substituted β-carbolines have
generated considerable synthetic interest 7 in recent times as
these are ubiquitous in pharmaceuticals and a number of
biologically active compounds. In particular, C-1 vinyl-
substituted β-carbolines provide easy access to di ﬀerent
alkaloids8 (komaroine, perlolyrine, etc.) and lead compounds 2c
and undergo RCM reactions 9a,b for the construction of
diﬀerent fused polycyclic sca ﬀolds present in biologically
active alkaloids 9a,c,d (i.e., ﬂavopereirine, 9a ﬂavocoryline, 9a
cordatanine,9c lutonins C and D 9d etc.). To our surprise,
scrutiny of the literature reveals only a few reports 2c,8a,10 on the
synthesis of such vinyl-substituted β-carbolines though a
number of methods are available for other C1-substituted
derivatives, achieved primarily via the oxidation of THBCs. 7
More speciﬁcally, the installation of the double bond at the C1
position of β-carbolines is usually made using palladium-
catalyzed coupling8a of 1-chloro-β-carbolines prepared through
multiple steps or a condensation reaction between the
derivatives of a harmine alkaloid and an aldehyde. 2c,10
Hence, development of a facile and general method for the
construction of 1-vinyl β-carbolines from readily available
precursors continues to be fascinating.
In continuation of our work 11 on palladium-catalyzed
synthesis of heterocycles of biological interest and in view of
the immense potential of the N-allenamide substrates in recent
synthetic transformations, 12 we envisioned that a palladi-
um(0)-catalyzed cyclocondensation between N-allenamides 6,
derived readily from N-propargylated tryptamine through base
(i.e., NaH) treatment, and aryl iodides 7 would a ﬀord 1-vinyl
THBCs 1 (Scheme 1 f). Furthermore, a straightforward base-
induced elimination and subsequent in situ oxidation of
products 1 could provide a general entry into the class of β-
carbolines 2 (Scheme 1 f). Our hypothesis proved to be viable
upon choosing appropriate catalyst and reaction conditions;
the results obtained so far are described below.

■ RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
The study was initiated by exploring the model reaction
between allenamide 6a and phenyl iodide 7a in DMF at 80 °C
utilizing 5 mol % of Pd(OAc) 2 and 12 mol % of PPh 3 in the
presence of 2.0 equiv of potassium carbonate 11d (Table 1 ,
entry 1); to our disappointment, the desired product 1aa was
not formed even with di ﬀerent organic and inorganic bases
(results not shown).
Use of Ag 2CO3 (2.0 equiv) as base did provide 1aa, albeit in
low yield ( Table 1 , entry 2); the yield could be improved
slightly (Table 1, entry 3) by employing Pd 2(dba)3 as catalyst.
To our delight, subsequent reactions ( Table 1 , entries 4 −8)
using other ligands showed that the use of the bulky t-Bu-
XPhos instead of PPh 3 completed the reaction within 1 h,
aﬀording the product 1aa with 71% yield ( Table 1 , entry 4).
Replacement of the phosphine ligand with a bidentate one
(i.e., t-Bu-XantPhos) improved the yield further to 75% ( Table
1, entry 5), but lowering of the reaction temperature to 70 °C
entailed longer reaction time (i.e., 3h) and reduced the yield to
some extent ( Table 1 , entry 6). Surprisingly, use of other
bidentate ligands such as Xantphos and N-XantPhos had
detrimental e ﬀects on this reaction, as minor amounts of
multiple undesired products were formed, diminishing the
yield of 1aa (Table 1 , entries 7 and 8). Use of other
palladium(0) catalysts like Pd(dba)
2 and Pd(PPh3)4 separately
resulted in moderate yields ( Table 1 , entries 9 and 10),
suggesting Pd2(dba)3 to be the best. Similarly, employing other
solvent systems both polar and nonpolar ( Table 1, entries 11 −
14) furnished the product in moderate yields (29 −40%) only.
Thus, the reaction conditions of entry 5 of Table 1 were found
to be optimal.
We next investigated the substrate scope to examine the
generality of this reaction. As can be seen from Table 2, a wide
range of allenamides 6 and aryl iodides 7 could easily
participate in the reaction, a ﬀording THBCs 1 within 1 h in
moderate to excellent yields (35 −95%). However, use of nosyl
(Ns) as a nitrogen protecting group in place of tosyl (Ts) in
the allenamide moiety of substrate 6 had a detrimental e ﬀect,
lowering the yield of products ( 1ba/1bb). Gratifyingly, the
reactions of 6a with a bulky 1-iodonaphthalene ( 7c) and 2-
iodothiophene ( 7d) were also successful, furnishing the
expected products 1ac and 1ad though in moderate yields
(55−60%). Aryl iodides, 7b and 7e, f bearing an electron-
withdrawing group at the para position performed better than
those ( 7g/7h) having an electron-donating group (compare
the yields of 1ab/1ae/1af vs 1ag/1ah). Surprisingly,
replacement of the N-methyl group (R
2 = Me) in allenamide
6a by a benzyl or allyl group hindered the reaction to some
extent, resulting in lower yields (37 −60%) of products ( 1ca/
1ch/1db/1de), though N-butyl (R 2 = Bu) in allenamide 6i
favored the reaction, furnishing the product 1ia in very good
yield (76%).
On the other hand, incorporation of a phenyl group in the
alkyl chain tethered to the C3 carbon of the indole moiety (R 1
= Ph) as in allenamide 6e delivered the product 1eb in good
yield (64%) and high diastereoselectivity (dr >99:1); even
placement of an additional functional group (X = NO 2/OMe)
at C-5 position of the indole worked equally well, a ﬀording the
desired products ( 1fb/1gb and 1ga, dr >99:1). Substituents at
the C1 and C4 positions in THBC ring of products 1eb, 1fb,
1gb and 1ga (see Table 2 ) were found to be in a cis-
relationship, which is in line with a previous report. 4e This
relative stereochemistry was established using NMR data
including NOESY experiments (for details, see Figures S6 and
S7).
We also explored the prospect of utilizing allenamide 6h
having a free NH group on the indole ring by executing the
reactions with iodobenzene ( 7a), methyl 4-iodobenzoate ( 7b),
and 4-iodoanisole ( 7h) separately; gratifyingly, the desired
products 1ha, 1hb, and 1hh were formed within 1 h albeit in
moderate yields (35 −45%). Notably, neither the aryl bromide
nor the allenamide 6 bearing a sulfonyl group (e.g., R
2 = Ts) at
the nitrogen atom of the indole ring was found to be reactive.
In addition, we became interested in checking the prospects
of acid-catalyzed cyclization of allenamide substrates 6.13 To
our pleasure, overnight exposure of allenamide 6a to 10 mol %
p-TsOH led to the formation of THBC 1a successfully albeit in
moderate yield ( Scheme 2 ).

Thereafter, a number of THBCs 1 were exposed to DDQ in
order to establish the generality of the protocol ( Table 4). The
reactions were found to be complete within 5 −8 h, and a range
of functional groups (e.g., Me, allyl, OMe, CO 2Me, F) were
compatible. Nevertheless, an electron-withdrawing group (F/
CO2Me) in the para position of the side chain phenyl ring
facilitated this reaction compared to electron-donating (Me/
OMe) groups (viz. 2c/2d vs 2b/2f). However, substitution at
the indole ring nitrogen had no signi ﬁcant eﬀect (viz. 2a vs 2e
and 2d vs 2g), though an N-methyl substituent expedited the
reactions compared to an N-benzyl or N-allyl group.
Interestingly, the THBC substrate containing a C5 methoxy
group (X = OMe) delivered the β-carboline 2h with the
highest yield (93%).
We then turned our attention to explore the scope of this
reaction. To our surprise, tweaking the conditions for the
reaction between allenamide 6h and aryl iodides 7 by replacing
Pd2(dba) 3 and Ag 2CO3 with Pd(PPh 3)4 and Cs 2CO3,
respectively ( Table 2 ), triggered a Friedel −Crafts-type allylic
alkylation15 (at C3 position of indole) resulting in the
generation of aza-spiroindolenines 9 (Scheme 3 ). Initially, we
selected four aryl iodides comprising iodobenzene ( 7a), methyl
4-iodobenzoate ( 7b), 4-iodoacetophenone ( 7i), and 4-
iodotoluene ( 7g) to obtain the corresponding products 9a
(63%), 9b (65%), 9i (61%), and 9g (56%), respectively, within
1−5 h; the unfavorable role of the electron-donating group in
the iodide substrate 7 was noticeable. Furthermore, products
9a (dr 1.5:1) and 9g (dr 2.2:1) were obtained as inseparable
mixtures of two diastereomers with moderate diastereoselec-
tivity as evident from their 1H NMR spectra (see Figures S8
and S9 ), while aryl iodides 7b/7i having an EWG group
triggered the formation of products 9b/9i with very good
diastereoselectivity (dr 9:1). Notably, correlation peaks from
NOESY revealed that Ha and He are on the same face of the
pyrrolidine ring, as Ha proton signals showed correlation with
He signals but not with those of Hf/g (see Figure 2 ). These
NOESY observations (for details, see Figure S10 amd Table
S5) clearly suggest that the relative stereochemistries are 3 R
and 11 S.

Napieralski cyclization and screened against cyclin-dependent

anticancer activities (in vitro) of these compounds including
11a, b and the synthesis of more examples of 11 and 12 are
currently underway in our laboratories.

resulting in the formation of palladium(II) −π-allyl complex
B.

■ CONCLUSIONS
In summary, we have developed an expeditious approach for
the general synthesis of C1-vinyl-substituted-THBCs 1 via
palladium (0)-catalyzed cyclocondensation between N-allenyl-
tryptamines 6 and aryl iodides 7. The reactions are fast,
compatible with various functional groups at di ﬀerent sites of
the reactants and utilize simple substrates. The THBC
products could easily be converted into the corresponding β-
carbolines 2 using DDQ. Tweaking the reaction conditions for
the synthesis of the THBCs 1 could provide a convenient entry
to the class of aza-spiroindolenines 9. Furthermore, synthetic
applications of the β-carboline products to the 1-aroyl- β-
carbolines 11a, b of pharmacological interest and the formal
total synthesis of eudistomins Y1 and Y2 are also
demonstrated. We believe that the method will be useful to
practitioners engaged in organic and medicinal chemistry.
■ EXPERIMENTAL SECTION
General Information. All solvents were distilled using a heating
mantle prior to use. Petroleum ether refers to the fraction boiling in
the range 60 −80 °C. Acetonitrile was dried over phosphorus
pentoxide, distilled, and stored over 3 Å molecular sieves in a sealed
container. Commercial grade dry DMF (dimethylformamide) and
toluene were used as solvents. All reactions were carried out under
argon atmosphere and anhydrous conditions unless otherwise noted.
Reactions were monitored by thin-layer chromatography (TLC) on
silica gel 60 F254 aluminum plates. To visualize the developed
chromatogram, we used UV absorbance or iodine exposure. For
puriﬁcation, column chromatography was performed using 100 −200
mesh silica gel.
1H and 13C NMR spectra were recorded on a 300, 400
or 600 MHz spectrometer using tetramethylsilane (TMS) as internal
standard. Chemical shifts ( δ) are given from TMS ( δ = 0.00) in parts
per million (ppm) with reference to the residual nuclei of the
deuterated solvent used [CDCl
3: 1H NMR δ = 7.26 ppm (s); 13C
NMR δ = 77.0 ppm]. Coupling constants ( J) are expressed in Hertz
(Hz), and spin multiplicities are given as s (singlet), d (doublet), dd
(double doublet), t (triplet), td (triple doublet), m (multiplet), and br
(broad). All
13C NMR spectra were obtained with complete proton
decoupling. Mass spectra were performed using ESI-TOF and EI
ionization mode. Crystallographic data were obtained using Bru ̈ker
Kuppa Apex 2 instrument.
Procedure for the Synthesis of N-Allenamides 6. N-
Allenamides 6 were synthesized in three steps starting from N-
protected tryptamine (see Scheme S1 ). After generation of N-
propargylated tryptamine ( S3), allenamides 6 can be derived easily
through base (i.e., KO tBu) treatment from S3.
General Procedure for the Synthesis of Acetylenes S2 from
S1 (See Scheme S1 ). The acetylene compound N-(2-(1H-indol-3-
yl)ethyl)-4-methyl- N-(prop-2-yn-1-yl)benzenesulfonamide ( S2a)5c
was prepared by a known literature procedure. Adopting the same
procedure, to a stirred solution of S1 (10 mmol) in acetone (25 mL)
under nitrogen was added K 2CO3 (2.8 g, 20 mmol), then 3-
bromopropyne (1.3 mL, 15 mmol) was added, and the mixture was
heated to re ﬂux for 24 −48 h. After completion of the reaction
(monitored by TLC), water was added to quench the base and then
extracted with ethyl acetate. The combined extracts were washed with
saturated salt water and dried over anhydrous sodium sulfate. After
removal of the solvent under reduced pressure, the crude product was
puriﬁed by column chromatography over silica gel (100 −200 mesh)

anhydrous AlCl3 (0.06 mmol) in dry toluene (1 mL) was stirred at rt
for 5 h for the generation of reported useful products 11a27 and 11b28
